Lesser silver smelt (Argentina sphyraena) exhibits a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 7% [GSI = 7%] when measured in waters maintained at a stable temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. This value, which reflects the relative allocation of body mass to reproductive tissues, was derived from specimens collected during the pre-spawning aggregation period in the northeastern Atlantic. Adult females of this species can attain a maximum total length of 35 centimeters [Li = 35 centimeters], representing the upper boundary of somatic growth observed in wild populations sampled over a decade of survey work. This ultimate length corresponds to an allometrically predicted ultimate female wet weight of 295.1 grams [Wwi = 295.1 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions fitted to a large series of mature individuals captured across the species' geographic range.

The onset of reproductive maturity in Argentina sphyraena is marked by the attainment of a total length at puberty of 12.5 centimeters [Lp = 12.5 centimeters], a threshold that typically coincides with the transition from the juvenile growth phase to the adult reproductive phase. Individuals at this length are estimated to have a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 11.2 grams [Wwp = 11.2 grams], based on the same allometric relationship used for adult mass estimation. Field observations indicate that puberty is generally reached within the second year of life, although local thermal regimes can influence the exact timing of gonadal recrudescence. The species exhibits a relatively early maturation strategy that permits rapid population turnover, an adaptation that may reflect the selective pressures of a variable pelagic environment where adult survival is not guaranteed. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this length at puberty is near the lower end of the range observed within the genus Argentina, highlighting a relatively fast life-history pace for this particular smelt.

Reproductive output in the lesser silver smelt begins with the production of small, pelagic eggs. The wet weight at birth, determined from the diameter of a fertilised ovum measuring approximately 800 micrometers, is calculated to be 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams]. This extraordinarily low neonatal mass reflects the tiny, yolk-dependent larvae that emerge following chorion rupture, a developmental mode common among marine teleosts that spawn numerous, small eggs to offset high larval mortality in the plankton. The egg diameter of 800 micrometers was obtained from measurements of freshly spawned oocytes collected from gravid females during a spring spawning survey. Such diminutive hatchlings are entirely lecithotrophic for the first several days after eclosion, relying on endogenous yolk reserves to sustain them until the onset of exogenous feeding and the critical transition to a pelagic larval existence. The low birth mass underscores a life-history strategy centered on high fecundity and minimal parental investment per offspring.

Under the thermal conditions characteristic of their native habitat, where water temperatures average 8 °C [T = 8 °C], the maximum longevity recorded for Argentina sphyraena is 16 years [am = 16 years]. This lifespan estimate was derived from otolith increment analysis of the oldest individuals captured during a long-term monitoring program in the Porcupine Seabight. A lifespan of 16 years is notably extended for a fish of this body size, especially when compared with other small pelagic species such as sprats or anchovies, which rarely exceed a decade. The relatively slow pace of senescence observed in this species may be linked to its cold-water thermal regime, which depresses metabolic rates and consequently slows the accumulation of cellular damage over time. This extreme longevity, combined with a moderate reproductive output and early maturation, positions the lesser silver smelt as a species with a distinctly slow life-history pace among its ecological peers.

The total length at puberty of 12.5 centimeters [Lp = 12.5 centimeters] marks a critical developmental threshold in Argentina sphyraena, after which individuals transition from primarily somatic growth to the allocation of resources toward gamete production. Correspondingly, the wet weight at that life stage is estimated at 11.2 grams [Wwp = 11.2 grams], a mass that supports the energetic demands of first gonadal maturation. The observed longevity of 16 years [am = 16 years] in 8 °C [T = 8 °C] waters is consistent with the slow metabolic rates typical of cold-water marine fishes; for instance, related deep-sea smelts in the genus Argentina exhibit similarly extended lifespans that are hypothesised to result from reduced predation pressure and low ambient temperatures. The ultimate female weight of 295.1 grams [Wwi = 295.1 grams] underscores a moderate adult body size that remains stable after the asymptotic length of 35 centimeters [Li = 35 centimeters] is reached. These life-history attributes, when considered together, depict a species that balances a relatively leisurely pace of development and aging with a reproductive strategy suited to an unpredictable pelagic environment. The interplay between early maturation and extended longevity, both modulated by the cold-water thermal regime, illustrates how Argentina sphyraena has evolved a life-history strategy that diverges markedly from that of many other small pelagic teleosts sharing its northeastern Atlantic habitat.
